 Mark Medina NBA Reporter Fact checked by: Sergey Demidov Updated: Oct 21, 2026, 7:32 PM Published: Oct 21, 2026, 6:31 PM 16 min read Editorial Standards Why Trust Us? Fred VanVleet missed all of last season with a torn right ACL. His longtime trainer, Mike Guevara, now says the Rockets will stack up wins with him back. In an interview with RG, Guevara walks through VanVleet’s rehab, the decision to skip the playoffs and why his impact goes beyond the box score.
 (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images)
 No longer will Fred VanVleet work under a cloud of uncertainty.
 No more surprising news about the nature of his right ACL injury . No more lengthy rehab. No more dashed hopes to return just in time for the Houston Rockets’ postseason run.
 After spending an entire offseason encouraged by how well his client strengthened his right knee, VanVleet’s personal trainer technically conceded uncertainty on what his numbers will look like in the 2026-27 season. But after witnessing VanVleet’s patient persistence and resilience, Mike Guevara remained bullish about one thing involving his client. That involves how VanVleet will affect the Rockets’ fortunes beginning with Wednesday’s game against the Dallas Mavericks (8:30 p.m. ET).
 “We’ll have a lot more W’s than L’s because Fred is back in the starting lineup,” Guevara told RG.org. Guevara spoke extensively to RG about VanVleet’s rehab and training, VanVleet’s initial hopes to return before the playoffs last season and his outlook on VanVleet’s upcoming season.  Editor’s note: The following one-on-one conversation has been edited and condensed. 
 Given that Fred was recovering from his injury, what did his offseason work with you entail? 
 Guevara: He tore his ACL just before the season last year in September. That meant that we had an initial goal to try to come back. It’s not unheard of for athletes to come back six to seven months after surgery. There were stipulations attached to that: that the Rockets were in good playoff position, the rehab went well and everything pointed in the right direction. That was initially the goal. But everybody rehabs differently. It just didn’t happen that way.
 So we had a traditional full year to get back to full strength and take our time and do it in a manner that didn’t feel rushed. So this offseason was primarily focused on making sure we hit all the major key performance indicators (KPIs) that an ACL rehab requires. That is dictated and subjected to thousands of ACLs that have been treated before his. That’s where all the data and strategy is based off of. There are case studies that mimic similar attributes — NBA point guard, 6-foot-4 and under and at a certain weight. That’s how they dictate all of these different KPIs. We had all summer to do that, so we didn’t need to rush. The pressure was down with trying to get back quickly. When you’re trying to get back to the playoffs, there is a little bit of pressure and a little bit of a push. But there was none of that.
 Fred escaped to San Diego for about 65 days. It’s probably the best place you can ever go to do a major training period. It’s peaceful. There are fewer distractions. The beaches are phenomenal. The food is phenomenal. There is great hiking. The air quality is better. It’s almost like the perfect place to go to. That’s where we decided to go based on Cam Hodges, one of the Rockets’ assistant coaches. He was one of the guys in charge of Fred’s on-court training. He’s the one that knew about this beautiful oasis.
 What were the main KPIs? 
 Guevara: Traditionally, it’s motion first. That is about the ability to move a joint in its full range of motion based on normative ranges. When you straighten your knee, there is a normative range. When you bend your knee, there is a normative range. Without full range of motion, bad things can start popping up. Then it’s about having basic, single-leg strength. That’s the ability to extend your leg with a large amount of force. You measure that to the other side. You want to get within 10% of the healthy side. Then it’s about having the ability to stop and decelerate.
 If you don’t have good, quality brakes and the ability to slow down, that’s when you can put yourself in a position to hurt yourself again. The ability to slow down requires the ability to change levels. If you have a really good strategy on changing levels and tolerance with changing levels at speed, you’re going to be safe. If I’m running full speed and I want to stop on a dime, but I can’t lower my center of mass? There is a lot of stress going into those joints. If I’m running full speed, I want to stop and be able to drop my hips. If not, I’m probably not going to be able to slow down well, or I’ll hurt myself. Deceleration is a huge KPI because it involves so many other movement skills and strength adaptation.
 Then the biggest KPI is the mental piece and repetition. It’s about consistently being in a space of randomness and chaos to build the confidence to trust the leg again. If I’m constantly thinking about my knee with every move that I make, that psychological noise is going to make me slower on the court, not see the court and not be myself. So it’s about consistently repping to get the psychological noise back to norm. With Fred at 6 feet and 200 pounds, that’s what makes him the best at what he does. He sees the court so well. He plays at a pace. He’s so calm under pressure. Between the ears is what he’s the best at mastering. So to get over that hump was the biggest one.
 Normally, you do a lot of isometric and pool work with Fred. Given this was a different kind of offseason, was Fred still doing those things? Or was it different stuff? 
 Guevara: It was a form of that. I still love isometrics. I still love pool work. But we’re not getting in the pools with dumbbells and jumping. He’s not as dynamic in the pool. It’s more or less an environment for recovery. So we did recovery workouts in the pool. Isometrics is a form of strength training. That’s going to train the brain, the nervous system and the muscles to feel safe in a specific range of motion. 
 If Fred doesn’t like being low, we’ll do some isometrics where he’s low. That will be the bridge from decelerating to playing on the basketball court.
 In another interview, Fred called you the “drill sergeant with charisma” during normal training sessions. How similar or different was your approach this summer? 
 Guevara: At this point, we were like seven or eight months out from surgery. So he’s really in training mode. With rehab, you have a connection more with the medical side. But since it was eight months out, it was less medical and more training. My personality and approach each day was “offseason grind, get-better mode.” It was push, push, push. Let’s try to squeeze the juice out of every single day and be mindful of redlining, but not overdoing it.
 What examples captured that challenge? 
 Guevara: I would be remiss not to mention another gentleman named Jason Biles [the Rockets’ head athletic trainer and director of athlete care and science]. He was there with us in San Diego. It was mostly under his direction. He was our captain. He drove the ship in terms of directing me on volume, exercise types and strategizing each type of day. He strategized each type of day — push hard on this day, and maybe not so much on this day.
 He gets a lot of credit because he’s the one that laid the road map out. Then he put me in a position to be good at what I’m good at. It was a team effort. Without him, I don’t know if we have as good of an understanding of objective load. He brought tools in that measured specific distance and specific change of direction. He brought tools that he could measure with and put inside shoes. He used that data to help us understand how to load the system on the court and how to load the system with speed and agility drills. It was very significant to our progression. We knew when to push and when not to, so it wasn’t random. It wasn’t based off how he felt. It was very specific to the numbers. I never used that before. So there is a lot of merit to the success of this rehab to Jason Biles and what he brought to the table. Jason was also working on the table with him and doing his physical therapy. He’s making sure that his range is good and his muscles feel good. I’m very thankful that we had him in our corner. They needed eyes on Fred that were representative of the Rockets. I’m on the team. But they still wanted somebody with Fred also to report back and give quality feedback on how everything was going.
 “I want to give as much credit to Fred as I can. He did everything he was asked to do. He showed up. He was a professional. He trained his butt off. We are definitely reaping the rewards and benefits of that. I also want to give credit to the team. It’s not about me at all. It’s about the team. If it wasn’t for the team, I don’t know if we’re as successful as we are.” At what point was it clear that Fred wouldn’t be able to return last season? 
 Guevara: Maybe around late April. The Rockets are about to play the Lakers in the first round [of the playoffs]. It felt like maybe Fred could come back, but it’s a risk. Any time you come back before nine months, it’s a risk. It’s in the data. It’s unequivocally proven that if you come back before nine to 12 months, it’s a big risk. So it was like, “Maybe we should take our time and be hesitant about coming back even if the Rockets get to the second round.” There are certain benchmarks you have to hit. He wasn’t on the court playing in contact at that time. So how could he go from playing contact to coming back into playoff basketball? Seven months out is a tall order to live up to. Once the surgeon said it would be a big risk to come back that early, we made a decision that was best for Fred.
 So this is literally just before the playoffs started? 
 Guevara: Yeah. The goal was to get back before the playoffs. But in order to get back and feel confident, he needed to have already played five-on-five contact against the video guys, the coaches and some of the younger guys. We weren’t doing that yet. So we thought the likelihood of getting to that moment in such a short amount of time would be low.
 How did you see Fred process that reality? 
 Guevara: He was fine with it. He’s a realist. He understands. He’s not going to BS himself. He saw where he was at in his recovery. He liked where he was at and was happy with where he was at, but he just wasn’t ready to go back to play in playoff basketball. That’s a whole other level. The intensity of playoff basketball is definitely different than the regular season. You definitely need a ramp-up.
 Given the severity of that injury, what jumped out to you on how Fred handled that news? 
 Guevara: What’s crazy is that when it initially happened, we all thought it was just a sprain. The following day, Fred was getting treatment and he was able to do single-leg squats. He was able to run. He was able to do all types of stuff. Then the MRI told him that he actually tore his ACL. So we were a bit confused. It was a shock-and-awe factor more than anything because of what he was capable of doing after the injury and before the MRI. We thought it was a sprain. We thought he would be out for four to six weeks. And then he would be ready to go. Then when he texted me, “I tore it,” I’m not sure what the right answer is to that question. The emotions are definitely high. This is the first injury that he’s ever had in his entire career. He’s never missed a basketball season since he started at 4 years old. So all of these feelings are pretty heavy.
 But Fred is probably one of the most emotionally sound people that I know, maybe even to a fault. He’s so even-keel that you can’t read him. This wasn’t any different. He didn’t have a huge despair of emotions. He didn’t have a huge drop-off. The way he approached rehab and training, he didn’t have a depressed presentation every day. Obviously, he wasn’t the happiest person in the building. But he showed up every day. He went through his treatment. He stayed in professional mode. He showed up for his teammates. And he was almost like an associate head coach on the bench. He sees the game in a different way and has a way to connect and socialize with his teammates at the level that they need. That’s a special trait.
 So when did Fred start training with you last season? 
 Guevara: That’s a good question. I didn’t do anything for the first three months. That was all physical therapy. I was around every single day, learning and helping in as much capacity as I could. But mainly, I was standing around and observing and being a student. I always tell people that it was more of an educational experience for me than anything. I feel pretty confident with rehabbing an ACL from early stage to late. But we didn’t really transition into strength and conditioning outside of physical therapy through the first three months. I think he was refreshed that he could do more things that he was used to doing. We had been training for four offseasons prior to that. Doing rehab from that perspective is very boring, monotonous and not mentally stimulating. So to be able to graduate and get to the early stage and start working with me was a bit refreshing. It was also painful. We started to do more complex training and really started to stress the body and the muscle. He was looking forward to that until we started to do it (laughs). It’s a love-hate relationship. But I think he was ready to get into that mode and was ready to get away from the treatment room.
 It was isometrics. We tried to reinforce motion, extension, flexion and the ability for the knee to move with a range with load. It’s one thing to bend your knee and strengthen your knee. But it’s another thing to bend your knee with resistance and straighten your knee with resistance. 
 That’s how you reinforce the brain’s ability to remember range of motion. So getting the instructions from the PT, Jason Biles, and allowing him to guide my programming on what we should be doing and what we should avoid. I then used my personal flair and creativity to make the athlete excited to come train so it doesn’t feel mundane and boring. I’m always trying to keep the training environment fun. But we still stay within the guardrails of what the PT wants us to do.
 The last thing I want to do is turn him into a bodybuilder or make him feel like he’s just a bodybuilder. That’s the creative side of training. How can I get this athlete to feel athletic even though we’re constrained and can’t do certain things like hop around, run or sprint? That’s something I’m always trying to consider, whether he’s healthy or not. How can I make this an exhilarating and engaging session without losing the focus of whatever tissue we try to load?
 Given all of Fred’s recovery and training work, what do you expect Fred’s season will be compared to how he was before his injury? 
 Guevara: Everyone is going to judge Fred on his numbers and shooting percentage. But one thing we will relish in and will champion is that “W-L” column. I think we’re going to have a lot of W’s. And it’s going to be because of the fact that Fred is back in the starting lineup. I don’t know if he’ll shoot the lights out or have an amazing assist-to-turnover ratio. I don’t know that to be true. I don’t know what’s going to happen. I, for sure, hope so and believe that he will. But what I do know is that we’re going to be a very, very good basketball team. I think we’ll have a lot more W’s than L’s because Fred is back in the starting lineup.
 So numbers aside, how do you think Fred will impact winning? 
 Guevara: It was evident the first day of training camp. He’s the loudest person on the floor. He’s organizing the offense. He demands so much out of our young guys with Jabari [Smith Jr.] and Alperen [Şengün]. He gives Kevin [Durant] a security blanket. Kevin doesn’t have to touch the basketball on every possession. He sets screens. He’s such a smart defensive player that he’s going to force turnovers. He’s going to be in the passing lane. He’s good at communicating. He slips screens. It’s so evident the impact he makes on the game immediately on the first day of training camp. That is how the wins are going to rack up. The guy is the definition of the floor general. He is the 6-foot, 200-pound floor general that is the biggest personality and leader on the floor. People can see that. People look to him for that. It’s a beautiful thing to see and watch.
